cards.title: Leveraging the solar revolution
cards.author: Ali Tauqeer Sheikh
cards.why: This is essential for understanding Pakistan's energy crisis, the role of climate policy, and the economic impacts of IMF-driven tariff adjustments.
cards.summary: Pakistan is experiencing an unplanned solar revolution driven by citizens seeking affordable energy amid high tariffs. Distributed solar has saved over $12 billion in fuel imports by February 2026 and provides significant electricity, despite government attempts to limit it. The author suggests moving beyond rooftop installations to a strategic second phase that maximizes the use of this green power.
key_facts: Pakistan installed nearly 22 gigawatts of rooftop solar capacity in two years.
Distributed solar avoided over $12 billion in oil and gas imports by February 2026.
Solar energy now supplies about one-third of the country's electricity when grid losses are considered.
Solar powers 52 percent of Pakistan's 1.83 million irrigation pumps.
Total investment in the solar transition is estimated at $14 billion.

vocab.meaning: The process of powering something with electricity.
A mechanism that allows solar users to feed excess energy back into the grid.
A beneficial result or advantage gained from an action.

text: AT COP31, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif told a high-level dialogue on electrification that “an extraordinary transition has already taken place” in Pakistan: nearly 22 gigawatts of rooftop solar in two years, “a quiet revolution by ordinary citizens seeking affordable power and a cleaner, more predictable future”. More than one in 10 motorcycles sold this year, he added, was electric.
He was right to showcase it. Few countries can match that speed. Fewer can accept that their citizens paid for it.

Nobody planned it: capacity payments rose whether plants ran or not, the rupee fell, and the 2023 IMF programme stopped the state hiding these costs in subsidies. Base tariffs doubled between FY22 and FY25, just as Chinese panels became cheap and loadshedding persisted. The IMF did not create the high cost of power. It made it visible, and achieved the revolution by accident, what policy had not.

The dividend is large. By the estimates of Ember, CREA and Renewables First, distributed solar avoided over $12 billion in oil and gas imports by February 2026, with $6.3bn more expected this year, and about 35 million tonnes of CO2 in FY25. Counting grid losses, it supplies about a third of the country’s electricity. On farms, solar runs 52pc of 1.83m irrigation pumps, almost entirely without state help. Banks financed less than 5pc of the $14bn invested. The official response has been to contain it, with a sales tax on panels and cuts to net metering .
A showcase needs a strategy. The leveraging should run on two tracks.
Phase one put panels on roofs; phase two must make that power go further.

The first is phase two. Phase one put panels on roofs; phase two must make that power go further. Rooftops have already displaced most of the daytime thermal power they can reach, so more panels alone bring falling returns. Three areas will win the game.

Storage, with a tariff that spreads the grid’s fixed costs fairly, so surplus daytime power serves the evening peak. Transport, where petrol imports are still growing: electric motorcycles reached 13pc of sales by August, already ahead of the New Energy Vehicles Policy’s schedule. The 30pc target should move from 2030 to 2028 for automobiles, two-wheelers, rickshaws and delivery fleets first, with battery-swap and charging corridors for bikes and freight planned along the motorways now. And solar mini-grids for the 40m people still without electricity.

The prize is worth the effort. Adding 3GW of distributed solar a year would lift avoided emissions to about 50m tonnes by 2030, as per Renew­ables First estimates, more than the power sector now emits. At this year’s rate, fuel import savings by then would approach $25bn. Electric bikes save less, but their savings will help poorer hou­seholds, which is where a transition survives or dies.
The second track is harder. If fiscal conditionality could transform mitigation by accident, what could adaptation measures achieve by design, without waiting for grants or loans?

Agriculture uses more than 93 per cent of the country’s freshwater, yet produces under $1 of output per cubic metre, against a global average near $17. Solar has made matters worse: once panels are paid for, pumping groundwater costs nothing at the margin. The rice area grew by about 30pc between 2023 and 2025, even as Punjab’s water tables fell. Flooded paddies also emit methane, so the same expansion that drains aquifers adds to emissions.
Islamabad and the provinces already hold the levers. Five would do the most.

First, conditional solarisation. Punjab already subsidises tubewell conversion; each should require drip or sprinkler irrigation and a flow meter. The Punjab Water Act 2019 allows new solar wells to be registered.
Second, volumetric abiana. The canal water charge is so low that sugarcane and rice grow where the water cannot support them. Charging by volume and crop is a provincial power, and it raises revenue.

Third, retargeted fertiliser support. IMF pressure ended most of the feedstock gas subsidy to urea plants in 2024. Blanket urea still invites overuse; the excess escapes as nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas, or leaches into groundwater. Tying the remaining support, including Kissan Card credit, to soil testing and slow-release coated urea would cut the waste and the fertiliser bill together.

Fourth, alternate wetting and drying for rice. Letting paddies dry between irrigations cuts both water use and methane. Punjab and Sindh can initiate this through their extension services and Kissan/Hari cards, with a low-carbon basmati label for buyers who increasingly ask about embedded emissions.

Fifth, a satellite-enforced no-burn rule. Tying Kissan Card eligibility and wheat procurement to satellite checks on residue burning, already run for smog, is an administrative change. Lahore would breathe cleaner air.

None of these needs a donor. The petroleum levy brought in a record Rs1.57 trillion in FY26, and the climate support levy is budgeted at Rs50bn this year. Ring-fencing a fixed share of the first, and all of the second, would fund them without waiting on donor cycles. The provinces, which own agriculture and irrigation, ran a combined cash surplus of Rs1.45tn last year, led by Punjab; only Balochistan’s was marginal.

Those surpluses are an IMF target, which brings the Fund back in. Its $1.4bn Resilience and Sustainability Facility already lists irrigation water pricing, but its water measures are hostage to influential interest groups. The two remaining reviews in 2027 can begin the shift; the successor programme should put adaptation at the centre, with these five as structural benchmarks carrying provincial timelines. The Fund’s leverage transformed Pakistan’s energy use by accident. It can now be used on water deliberately.

Some things need capital: flood protection, climate-proofed infrastructure, livestock systems that cut methane. That is where concessional finance belongs. A country that has done the rest with its own instruments makes a far stronger case for it.

Phase one happened by accident. Phase two cannot. Islamabad should design the next transformation, in water as well as power, rather than wait for the next IMF programme to force it. The first revolution cut Pakistan’s fuel bill and emissions. The second can make the country resilient.
The writer is a climate expert.
Published in Dawn, November 19th, 2026

cards.title: Exchange rate & other protections
cards.author: Khurram Husain
cards.why: It provides a clear explanation of REER and exchange rate dynamics, which are fundamental concepts in Pakistan's economic policy discussions.
cards.summary: The column discusses the debate over Pakistan's exchange rate and the competitiveness of exports. It explains the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) as a tool to measure cost alignment with trading partners. The author notes that industries are unusually silent on devaluation, despite experts claiming it would boost competitiveness.
key_facts: The Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) measures a country's exchange rate alignment adjusted for inflation against trading partners.
A REER value of 100 indicates theoretical alignment between a country's business costs and its competitors.
A REER above 100 is considered overvalued, potentially making exports less competitive.
A REER below 100 is considered undervalued, potentially favoring exporters.

vocab.meaning: Reduced the official value of a currency.
A position of agreement or cooperation.

cards.title: La nuora Italiana
cards.author: F.S. Aijazuddin
cards.why: Useful for understanding contemporary Indian political history and the influence of the Nehru-Gandhi family.
cards.summary: This column reviews the memoirs of Sonia Gandhi, titled 'Belonging: a Journey of Love'. It chronicles her transition from an Italian homemaker to the long-serving leader of the Indian National Congress. The text reflects on the personal tragedies and political pressures faced by the Nehru-Gandhi dynasty.
key_facts: Sonia Gandhi served as president of the Indian National Congress from 1998 to 2017 and 2019 to 2022.
Sonia Gandhi married Rajiv Gandhi in 1968.
Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated by an LTTE suicide bomber in 1991.
Annie Besant was the first female president of the Indian National Congress in 1917.

vocab.meaning: Assistance and support in times of hardship.
The process of becoming part of a different culture or group.

cards.title: Arab blood
cards.author: Muhammad Ali Siddiqi
cards.why: Provides a critique of regional security dynamics and the lack of unity among Arab nations.
cards.summary: The author examines the internal conflicts and divisions within the Arab world. He argues that disunity hampers the regional response to challenges like the war in Yemen. The article highlights the creation of opposing defense alliances and the vulnerability of the region to external pressures.
key_facts: The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement was signed on August 7, 2026.
The author notes the intense conflict between Saudi-led forces and Houthi groups in Yemen.
Regional tensions are exacerbated by the formation of conflicting defense alliances.

vocab.meaning: A thing that comes before another and influences its development.
A military force that is raised from the civil population.
